candidato.titulo: Lactation drug could reduce breast cancer risk after childbirth, study suggests
candidato.resumo: An international team of scientists has found that a lactation drug could reduce the risk of breast cancer in mothers after childbirth. Cabergoline, a medication used to stop milk production after pregnancy loss or when breastfeeding is not possible, is generally well tolerated by patients with few side effects. But it may also offer unexpected benefits.

texto_fonte:
Lactation drug could reduce breast cancer risk after childbirth, study suggests
An international team of scientists has found that a lactation drug could reduce the risk of breast cancer in mothers after childbirth. Cabergoline, a medication used to stop milk production after pregnancy loss or when breastfeeding is not possible, is generally well tolerated by patients with few side effects. But it may also offer unexpected benefits.
The study, published in Cancer Discovery, analyzed health records from Spain and Norway, including more than 150,000 women with information on whether they had used cabergoline.
Women who had the medication to suppress milk production were around 70% less likely to develop breast cancer in the years that followed, compared with those who did not receive cabergoline.
This finding mirrored what the researchers found in mice. They tested a single dose of cabergoline in mice carrying BRCA1 and TP53 mutations, which are associated with aggressive forms of breast cancer, and tumor incidence rates fell by about half.
"Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death among younger women, and the majority of these cancers occur during the years after pregnancy," said study co-lead Dr. Christopher Maxwell, professor in UBC's faculty of medicine and investigator at BC Children's Hospital Research Institute.
"This is particularly true for women at high risk of breast cancer. But our findings suggest there may be an opportunity to reduce that risk with an existing drug by helping the breast complete a natural process that happens after breastfeeding ends."
Like a fruit tree preparing for winter
After a woman stops breastfeeding, the breast undergoes a major cleanup process called "involution."
Maxwell likened it to a fruit tree. In spring and summer, the tree grows branches and produces blossoms and eventually fruit. Once the fruit is gone, the tree sheds what it no longer needs and prepares for the next season.
Similarly, during pregnancy, hormone levels rise and the milk-producing structures within the breast branch out, creating a 'ductal tree.' But once breastfeeding ends, those cells are no longer needed and the breast undergoes involution to remove excess tissue.
"We think of involution as the breast's version of winter," said Maxwell. "It's a period when structures that were needed for pregnancy and breastfeeding reset for the future."
But the researchers found that this cleanup process can be incomplete in the experimental mice, leaving behind cells that may become cancerous.
Cabergoline appears to help complete that transition by accelerating the breast's natural post-weaning process. In mouse studies, it reduced potentially precancerous tissue, shrank the ductal area, reduced cell growth, and boosted immune cells responsible for clearing damaged cells.
Clinical trial in the works
With one in eight women in Canada developing breast cancer in their lifetime, the researchers say new prevention strategies are urgently needed.
"We think the period after breastfeeding is an important window for prevention," said study co-lead Dr. Jesús Perez-Losada, a researcher at the Cancer Research Center, a joint institute of the Spanish National Research Council and the University of Salamanca.
"There is a unique opportunity to target involution, the natural process that begins after weaning. This is not about changing a woman's breastfeeding plans; any preventive intervention would be considered only after breastfeeding has ended."
The next step for the researchers is to test cabergoline in clinical trials and determine whether the benefits observed in mice can be confirmed in people. The multinational research team aims to conduct a clinical trial spanning multiple countries.
Women with a BRCA1 mutation will be recruited through high-risk clinics and will choose how long they want to breastfeed. After weaning, they will receive either cabergoline or a placebo while researchers monitor biological markers linked to future breast cancer risk.
It's a promising avenue because current preventive measures for women at high risk include hormone therapy or surgery, both of which can have significant physical and emotional side effects.
If successful in clinical trials, the drug's existing approval by regulatory agencies including Health Canada and the European Medicines Agency could accelerate its path to use as a breast cancer prevention strategy.
Publication details
Cabergoline Suppresses Postpartum Breast Cancer by Enhancing Mammary Gland Involution in Brca1-Mutant Mice and Is Associated with Reduced Risk in Younger Women, Cancer Discovery (2026). DOI: 10.1158/2159-8290.CD-26-0187
Journal information: Cancer Discovery

candidato.titulo: Candida auris copies its entire genome to survive antifungal treatment, research reveals
candidato.resumo: New research has revealed an unexpected new mechanism through which the killer fungus Candida auris is resisting antifungal drug treatment. A team led by the University of Exeter and City St George's, University of London, discovered that the fungus creates multiple versions of its entire genome, including mutating a gene that plays a role in cell wall integrity, called "Crazy-one" (CRZ1).

texto_fonte:
Candida auris copies its entire genome to survive antifungal treatment, research reveals
New research has revealed an unexpected new mechanism through which the killer fungus Candida auris is resisting antifungal drug treatment. A team led by the University of Exeter and City St George's, University of London, discovered that the fungus creates multiple versions of its entire genome, including mutating a gene that plays a role in cell wall integrity, called "Crazy-one" (CRZ1).
The study is set to appear in Nature Communications and is currently available on the bioRxiv preprint server.
Study authors say their findings unlock a new mechanism that allows Candida auris to adapt to antifungal treatment and survive, which could lead to new ways to tackle the fungus.
Candida auris was only described for the first time in 2008, and its origins remain a mystery. Since it emerged, outbreaks have been reported on every continent, in more than 60 countries in total, including the U.K. It has been named a global public health threat and is on the World Health Organization's critical priority fungal pathogens list.
A deadly threat in intensive care
Study first author Dr. Hugh Gifford, clinical lecturer at the University of Exeter's MRC Centre for Medical Mycology, is also an intensive care physician. He said, "Candida auris is rare in the general population, but it's a deadly threat to patients in intensive care units. It clings to patient skin and surrounding equipment and can be transmitted from person to person—it's incredibly hard to eradicate. If infection enters a vulnerable patient's bloodstream, there is a 45% death rate.
"Outbreaks in intensive care units have been costly and highly disruptive. One unit in the U.K. had to close and undergo complete refurbishment to stop the outbreak, while another outbreak was estimated to cost £1 million to control."
An accidental discovery of drug survival
The research team was initially testing for drug resistance when a researcher accidentally left plates of cells incubating for longer than the required test period. The researcher returned to find that cells had unexpectedly grown during this additional time period. They were surprised to find that further testing showed the deadly fungus had survived antifungal treatment by creating multiple versions of its own genome, thereby increasing its chances of mutating to evade the drug and survive.
Dr. Sarah Murphy, former postdoctoral researcher at City St George's University of London and co-first author, said, "We initially set out to investigate why antifungal drugs weren't working to kill Candida auris, despite laboratory tests showing that they were not resistant and that the drugs should have been effective. We were surprised to discover an entirely new mechanism for this fungus to survive—particularly with luck playing a big part in the discovery.
"We tested the fungus against very high concentrations of antifungal drugs. We were amazed to find there was a tiny population of cells that appeared over several days and continued to grow. Our discovery means we need to now look at new ways of treating people and eradicating this deadly fungus from hospitals."
Genome copies help the fungus hedge bets
Expanding further on the finding, Gifford said, "This study had a number of surprising elements. First, we did not identify any of the DNA mutations that we might have expected. Antifungal drugs target the enzymes that make cell walls, so that fungi die by shriveling, exploding or not being able to grow. Somehow, these fungi had survived antifungal drugs, and we needed to find out why.
"We were surprised to find that surviving cells had made multiple copies of their entire genome. This is a trick that other fungi have used in the past, but not one that is well known in C. auris. In fact, there were two populations, some growing slowly, others growing more rapidly. We call it 'bet-hedging' when a bug uses multiple tactics to increase its chances of developing resistance and evading treatment."
The team found that the more rapidly growing cells contained a wide range of mutations in a gene that has been studied in other organisms for its role in governing cell wall synthesis, called "Crazy-one" (CRZ1). Further tests confirmed the rapid growth of CRZ1 mutants and that their cell walls appeared to be unaffected by antifungal drugs.
Combining treatments to counter fungal adaptation
Researchers are now looking at options including the use of antifungal drugs in combination, which is being addressed via the Exeter-led UKRI-funded Fungi-CARE program, also in partnership with colleagues at City St George's.
Senior author Tihana Bicanic, professor of infectious diseases and mycology at the School of Health & Medical Sciences at City St George's, University of London, said, "We now believe that fungal infections are more complicated than previously thought. Multiple populations may exist during infection. New and emerging human fungal infections, like Candida auris, essentially have a Swiss Army knife of innovation with their own genome, leading to stepwise adaptation and drug resistance.
"The implication of these results is that we now know a new mechanism of evolution that weakens our antifungal drug arsenal. So, we are sounding the alarm for the need to make better antifungal drugs and urgently address our ability to prevent fungal deaths."
Publication details
FKS1/2-variant independent mechanisms underlying the emergence of resistance in echinocandin-refractory Candida auris infections, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76954-x. On bioRxiv: www.biorxiv.org/content/10.648 … /2026.01.17.700071v1

candidato.titulo: Agility chooses Nyobolt for ultra-fast charging for Digit 5 humanoid
candidato.resumo: Nyobolt is providing power technology for Digit 5 that enables Agility's humanoid to work up to 20 hours a day. The post Agility chooses Nyobolt for ultra-fast charging for Digit 5 humanoid appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
One of the challenges that humanoid robot designers face is power management. Agility Robotics Inc. today said it is working with Nyobolt on a fast-recharge battery system for its Digit 5 system. The technology will allow the robot to work more than 20 hours in a day, the companies claimed.
“For our customers, Digit’s uptime is the business case,” stated Daniel Diez, chief business officer at Agility. “Digit 5 will deliver more than 20 hours of productive work in a 24-hour day, more than two full shifts. That’s the kind of gain that materially improves the value customers get from Digit and the economics of deploying a humanoid robot fleet. Nyobolt’s ultra-fast charging technology gets us there, and it’s one of the pieces that makes Digit 5 ready for full-scale operation.”
Founded in 2015, Agility said Digit is “the first multi-purpose, human-centric robot that is ‘Made for Work’ and commercially deployed today.” The Salem, Ore.-based company said it has accumulated more than 65,000 of real-world operations. Last month, it released Digit 5 with new legs and acknowledged that it is considering wheeled locomotion.
Nyobolt builds batteries for fast charging
Founded in 2019, Nyobolt said it has combined proprietary anode materials, advanced battery cell design, and integrated power electronics to enable fast charging, high power density, reduced weight, and extended lifecycles. The Cambridge, U.K.-based company said its technology enables demanding industrial applications and reduces downtime, a key constraint in robot utilization.
Nyobolt said its patent portfolio and global footprint support AI datacenters, physical AI, and mobility applications while reducing the total cost of ownership. In May 2026, the company achieved a $1 billion valuation by raising $60 million including support from Symbotic Inc.
“Nyobolt’s technology was chosen because Digit 5 will need more power from a smaller, lighter pack in environments where reliability isn’t optional,” said Sai Shivareddy, co-founder and CEO of Nyobolt. “Agility set an exceptionally high bar for what a battery has to withstand in live warehouse and manufacturing environments, and this partnership shows what’s possible when ultra-fast charging is engineered for the toughest conditions in physical AI.”
Digit 5 features longer runtime for humanoid customers
Agility described Digit 5 as its first humanoid robot designed to work in close proximity to people safely and at scale. It will include a new battery system that delivers 90 minutes of runtime and charges in just nine minutes. This 10:1 run-to-charge ratio is an improvement from Digit 4’s 2:1 ratio.
The company asserted that this will let Digit 5 customers target longer operating windows, more productive shifts, and more demanding task sequences. Agility said this battery performance, combined with its experience with commercial deployments, will strengthen Digit’s value proposition for warehouse, distribution, and manufacturing operations.
Agility said it expects early access to Digit 5 equipped with Nyobolt’s technology to begin in the first half of 2027. Availability will increase over the following six to nine months, it added.
Agility execs prepare for merger, to speak at RoboBusiness
Agility plans to go public through a merger with special-purpose acquisition firm (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp XI. In July, Agility opened a software and capabilities hub in Fremont, Calif., to accelerate physical AI development.
Earlier this month, the company partnered with FORT Robotics (which is also entering a SPAC deal) to advance robot safety. In addition, Agility CEO Peggy Johnson has joined Project Meridian, a U.S. Department of War initiative to investigate the future of warfare and inform long-term investment priorities.
At RoboBusiness 2026 next week in Santa Clara, Calif., Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility, will participate in the opening keynote on “The Next 20 Years of Robotics.” On Day 2 of the event, Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer of Agility, will participate in a keynote panel on the “State of Humanoids.” Register now to attend.

candidato.titulo: Seven stable kernels for Thursday with fix for critical vulnerability
candidato.resumo: Greg Kroah-Hartman has announced the release of the 7.2.11 , 6.18.57 , 6.12.113 , 6.6.159 , 6.1.190 , 5.15.223 , and 5.10.272 stable kernels. This series includes, among other things, a fix for a critical vulnerability ( CVE-2026-99999 ). The flaw in skb_checksum_help() would allow an IPv4 packet with bad checksum metadata to " corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of mischief " in the words of patch author Michael S. Tsirkin. As usual, all users are advised to upgrade.

candidato.titulo: We tested the RTX Spark Superchip in Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra
candidato.resumo: We've tested Nvidia's RTX Spark against the latest and greatest from Apple and AMD to see how Nvidia's efforts to transform the PC for the agentic AI era stack up.

texto_fonte:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced the RTX Spark platform with the grand ambition to “reinvent the PC” back at Computex 2026. By pairing the GB10 Superchip with a version of Windows on Arm tailored for the secure and contained execution of local AI agents, Nvidia and its partners at Microsoft, Dell, HP, MSI, Lenovo, and Asus are all hoping to pave the way to a future where the PC is an active, autonomous companion for work and creation.
The hardware foundation for that vision of the future is now in place. Last week, we flew out to San Francisco to get all the details on the RTX Spark platform, and we returned home with Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra in top-end trim to put it all to the test.
This system has the full RTX Spark Superchip with 20 CPU cores and 6144 CUDA cores alongside 128GB of LPDDR5X-9400 RAM, and I’ve been putting it through its paces over the past week to see just what it can do.
The embargoes for the RTX Spark launch are a bit peculiar. Today, we’ll be sharing our broad experience with the Spark platform, as well as competitive performance evaluations, but not any system-specific results such as battery life, build or display quality, or other details of that nature. We have other RTX Spark laptops in the Tom’s Hardware labs, and detailed reviews of those systems will be coming soon.
No, this approach doesn’t make a lot of sense when the experience of a mobile platform is intimately and inextricably tied to the specific implementation of that chip in a particular laptop design. And we know that battery life is the first and foremost concern of many interested in this platform. But again, all that information is coming soon.
For this first round of testing, we compared the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark against two systems. The first is a 14" MacBook Pro with Apple's highest-end M5 Max SoC inside. That Mac has a 40-core GPU and an 18-core CPU, as well as 128 GB of LPDDR5X RAM. We don't have a mobile Ryzen AI Max+ 395 system in the labs right now, but we do have AMD's compact Ryzen AI Halo as a source of fresh data with the latest ROCm stack and llama.cpp builds.
Local AI performance
Judging local AI performance is a constantly moving target, and this review is no different. Our past testing has exercised the prompt processing and token generation phases of AI inference separately, with the understanding that a system that's fast at both those phases provides the best experience.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
But in an agentic workflow, that benchmarking technique doesn't capture the total time required to complete a task across all the inference turns needed to reach a particular goal. To capture that entire end-to-end time, the folks at Artificial Analysis have developed a new benchmark, AgentPerf-local, that precisely replays inference traces across several agentic AI tasks. The value of this approach should make immediate sense: the faster an AI agent finishes a job, the more productive a system can be.
So instead of presenting raw time-to-first-token and tokens-per-second figures, as we have in the past, we’re sharing time-to-completion values as we would for more traditional CPU and content creation benchmarks.
Again, local AI benchmarking is a continuous work in progress, so let us know what you think of this approach, and we’ll take that feedback into account as we continue to develop our methods.
We ran AgentPerf-local with two compatible models: the dense Qwen 3.8-27B, which is popular as one of the most intelligent local models available for its size, and the Qwen 3.6 35B A3B mixture-of-experts model, which is less intelligent but easier for a wide range of systems to run quickly. We used the latest build of llama.cpp as our inference backend and built it from source on each test system to take advantage of CUDA, Metal, or ROCm acceleration, as appropriate.
Let’s look at Qwen 3.8 27B’s behavior first. We used Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of the model. We ran it with DFlash2 speculative decoding on the RTX Spark and MacBook Pro, and with Qwen 3.8 27B’s built-in MTP on the Ryzen AI Halo for the best performance.
As we found in our benchmarking of Apple's Mac Studio with the M4 Max SoC, memory bandwidth is only one constraint for local AI performance. Despite its memory bandwidth advantage on paper, the M5 Max MacBook Pro still ends up taking about 25% longer to finish the AgentPerf benchmark with Qwen 3.8 27B than the Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark.
Part of that may be down to software maturity, but it's also worth remembering that our Surface Laptop Ultra is a 15" system with a much larger 140W power adapter versus the 14" MacBook Pro's 96W charger.
The 16" M5 Max MacBook Pro also comes with a 140W adapter, and we'd be curious to see whether the extra power and higher thermal headroom afforded by that system’s larger chassis help close the gap here. But in any event, the RTX Spark platform is the fastest overall at this task today.
Meanwhile, AMD's nearly two-year-old Ryzen AI Max+ 395 just can't keep up with either of these newer systems in this demanding test. It needs about twice as long to finish our agentic tests with Qwen 3.8 27B as either the RTX Spark or the MacBook Pro do, at a whopping 40 minutes.
The fact that the Ryzen AI Halo is a mini desktop form factor rather than a notebook doesn’t much matter to these results, as any power and thermal headroom that design might afford can’t possibly overcome the performance gap here.
Next up, we have the lighter-weight Qwen 3.6 35B A3B. We ran Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of this model with MTP enabled.
The Surface Laptop Ultra ends up completing this test in just eight minutes, or about 25% faster than the 14” MacBook Pro’s 10 minutes. This test is also much friendlier to the Ryzen AI Halo, which finished the benchmark in a more reasonable 13 minutes. But that just emphasizes that you have to trade away model intelligence to get a reasonable level of performance out of Strix Halo.
AMD has recently gone on a publicity blitz to highlight the relatively low cost of entry for Strix Halo systems versus DGX Spark desktops and now RTX Spark laptops. But if time is money, and getting more intelligent tokens out of your local AI system faster means more potentially profitable agentic work gets done, then a more expensive system upfront will be able to do more of that work and potentially generate more value over time.
Gaming performance: first impressions
Despite its RTX branding and the emphasis Nvidia places on its 6144-CUDA-core GPU (or 48 SMs), the RTX Spark platform faces some tough challenges for gaming. Most games available today are not going to be natively compiled for its Arm CPU, and even for those that might be, the maximum 300 GB/s of shared memory bandwidth the platform offers is well below that of even the RTX 5060 Mobile's dedicated 384 GB/s feeding 26 SMs.
The entire GB10 SoC is competing for a relatively small amount of memory bandwidth, and because graphics is generally a memory-bandwidth-bound workload, that's not a great start for feeding all of those SMs in games.
I started my gaming explorations with Gears of War: E-Day. In this exceptionally CPU-heavy game, it's clear that the baseline performance of the Grace CPU cores and the added overhead of the Prism x86 emulator are doing this title no favors.
GPU utilization only reaches the 85% mark on average at a near-1080p (1908x1272) render resolution with the High preset and 2X framegen, and we saw at least one major hang during a map transition that was less than confidence-inspiring for an immersive experience as we progress further into the game.
Because of its CPU dependence, Gears is probably a worst-case scenario for this platform, but the fact remains that it's not a great experience, and turning down settings or lowering upscaling input resolutions just exacerbates the CPU-boundedness of this title. If any game could use a native Arm build, this is the one.
Control Resonant is significantly less dependent on the CPU, but that just means that the other potential gaming shortcomings of the RTX Spark Superchip seem to come into play.
After struggling a bit to achieve a solid frame rate and input latency at the Surface Laptop Ultra's native 3270x2180 output resolution even with DLSS upscaling, I found that running the game in windowed mode at 2560x1440 with DLSS Performance upscaling, the High preset, and MFG 3X to keep frame rates near the Surface Laptop Ultra's 120Hz refresh rate provided better results. (This system's tall 3:2 aspect ratio means that 16:9 fullscreen games don't cleanly scale up.)
But even then, input latency was above what I would consider acceptable on our standard GPU test rig, and enabling ray tracing at all dipped frame rates and spiked input latency even further, so I had to stick to raster-only rendering for the best results.
Overall, my early RTX Spark gaming verdict is that you can do it, and you can have a fine enough time, but it is not the primary focus of this platform. Gaming performance with the relatively limited memory bandwidth of the RTX Spark Superchip, combined with the system's CPU performance and the overhead of Prism emulation, mean that you'll be searching for a narrow range of settings where baseline frame rates, upscaling, image quality, and the smoothness boost of frame generation still yield acceptable input latency.
When I first approached gaming on this platform, I had expected that DLSS upscaling would be a required part of the experience, but in practice, you really need to lean on DLSS Frame Generation, as well, whether that's for added smoothness (as in Gears of War) or for both smoothness and the benefits of Nvidia Reflex due to developer choices behind the scenes (as in Control Resonant).
Even with Reflex, though, the Grace CPU generally seems to deliver input latencies significantly higher than I'm used to on our Ryzen 7 9800X3D test rig, and it's hard to get them much lower in these AAA titles by tweaking settings.
If you demand the lowest input latency and the highest performance with cutting-edge games, especially if you plan to enable RT, a separate gaming laptop with a dedicated RTX 50-series GPU will still provide a superior experience. And if you just don’t care about local AI at all, that advice applies even more strongly.
Bottom line
Nvidia's RTX Spark is an ambitious new PC platform for the traditional workloads of today and the potential agentic AI work of tomorrow. How often do we see an entirely new player try to elbow into the crowded and competitive PC space, especially one with a sweeping vision for how the PC will be used in the years to come? An incremental move this is not.
Our general performance tests and new agentic AI tests show that despite providing merely solid CPU performance and relatively low bandwidth for a unified memory architecture on paper, the Blackwell GPU on board GB10 has enough AI horsepower in practice to let the RTX Spark platform come out ahead of Apple's latest top-end M5 Max and AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395, aka Strix Halo, SoCs.
Whether you choose the highly intelligent dense Qwen 3.8 27B model and trade raw speed for intelligence, or make the opposite trade with the lighter and faster Qwen 3.6 35B A3B, the RTX Spark comes out on top. That bodes well for pairing popular agents like Hermes with intelligent local models on this platform.
But Nvidia's mission to reinvent the PC isn't a total grand slam in this first iteration.
First, this platform won't replace a dedicated gaming laptop. Even for those who only game on the side and have more forgiving standards for frame rates and input latency, the RTX Spark's gaming performance may not measure up to expectations.
When you put the overhead of Prism x86 emulation on top of the merely adequate performance of the Grace CPU, it’s clear that the Spark platform will have to work hard to keep up in the vast range of games that don’t have an Arm port.
The CPU-heavy Gears of War: E-Day is particularly unkind to the Prism-on-Grace stack, but even when a title like Control Resonant doesn't lean so heavily on the CPU, the limited and shared memory bandwidth of the GB10 SoC still poses an obstacle to cranking settings to the max despite the large amount of theoretical compute horsepower on tap.
We're also still waiting for Windows to fully catch up to Nvidia's ambitions for secure, manageable local agents. Our laptop expert Andrew Freedman and I couldn't test Microsoft's secure agentic AI promises within Windows 11, as the supporting features that Microsoft and Nvidia have promised to that end just aren't ready yet.
Still, for a first-generation mobile platform that joins complex silicon IP from multiple design teams onto one chip and relies on several OEM partners to bring it to life in highly integrated notebook form factors, the maturity of the RTX Spark platform is an impressive achievement. (Take it from someone who has seen a couple of rough product launches from the inside.)
Over the past week, I've been using the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra as I would any other Windows laptop, and aside from a couple of tiny paper cuts, I have mostly just gotten my work done as I would with any other computer. And that’s a great — albeit a very, very expensive — place to be as the local agentic AI future coalesces.
Perhaps the biggest challenge for the RTX Spark platform is that the eye-watering price tags for the range of systems available at launch still buy a lot of cloud tokens from OpenAI and Anthropic. Emphasis on a lot. The Surface Laptop Ultra we tested lists for $5899 with only 1TB of storage, and lead times for that system are already out to late December.
If you're not as concerned about keeping sensitive data out of those labs’ clouds, or you don't expect to run afoul of acceptable usage policies, you'll get much smarter tokens much faster than you will from a local token factory like the RTX Spark, and you can get them on most any reasonably powered traditional PC you have available.
But if you're surfing the AI wave on local hardware for reasons of privacy, offline model availability, freedom to tinker, or just because you think it's cool, the RTX Spark platform blends the memory capacity, compute performance, and software resources you need to get there with the familiarity and broad compatibility of Windows on top. The fact that Nvidia, Microsoft, and their partners have delivered such a capable, compatible, and polished platform even in its first at-bat should put the rest of the PC industry on notice.
Nvidia’s efforts to reshape personal computing will face strong headwinds in the immediate future from the sky-high DRAM and NAND price hikes that the company’s own Vera Rubin rollout is partially responsible for. Perhaps when the dust settles in the next two to three years, and products built around the next-generation RTX Spark Superchips arrive, we can more confidently assess whether the company has accomplished its goal.
For now, the RTX Spark feels like a platform for those who fervently believe that open AI models will continue to get more intelligent within relatively small memory footprints, and that those potential future improvements are worth a hefty chunk of change to get ready for today. Maybe that's a smart bet in a world where compute is an increasingly precious resource. But unless you're a true believer with cash to burn, our first impressions suggest that you should wait until Microsoft and Nvidia fully lay the software foundation needed for this platform to deliver on its promises.
As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

candidato.titulo: Beat light pollution with these six portable telescopes
candidato.resumo: Sick of skyglow spoiling your stargazing? These six telescopes are portable enough that you can easily pack them away and seek out darker skies.

texto_fonte:
Light pollution is the astronomer's biggest enemy, especially if you're gazing into deep space. And while some of the best telescopes can make a difference, there's no way to eliminate it. That's why, if you want to observe the cosmos without obstruction, you need to seek out darker skies, get a smart telescope or combine the two.
You don't have to book a flight to a dark sky reserve; just traveling away from suburbia can be enough. That's where portable telescopes come in. Set one up in a field, for example, and you'll get a vastly improved view of the cosmos. Galaxies, nebulas and other deep space objects become more detailed when they're not washed out by skyglow.
We've picked out six telescopes you can take on the road: Some, such as the DwarfLab Dwarf Mini, are small enough you could even put them in a backpack and hop on your bicycle.
All but one are smart telescopes, meaning that when you do get to your desired location, you can pick from a list of stellar sights to home in on. And while they may be portable, they're powerful with it.
So, beat light pollution and say hello to stunning views of the night sky.
Chris is a freelance journalist who, aside from covering games and gaming-related tech, has a taste for horror, sci-fi and the post-apocalyptic. As well as Space.com, you can find his work at The Escapist, GameSpew (where he’s the morning news writer) and more. You can follow him on Twitter @MarmaladeBus.

candidato.titulo: FirstQFM Model Cuts Single-Qubit Gate Times by 33% on QuantWare Processor
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — FirstQFM today announced results from applying FirstQFM’s quantum foundation model to a QuantWare superconducting quantum processor at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center (IQCC). FirstQFM’s foundation model builds on top of Quantum Machines’ native calibration stack, and generated single-qubit gates that reduced execution time by 33% on a QuantWare Contralto-D21 QPU. […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- FirstQFM applied its quantum foundation model to a 21-qubit QuantWare superconducting processor at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center, reducing single-qubit gate execution time by 33% without reducing gate fidelity.
- The model generated custom pulse-level gate implementations from existing calibration data and identified five qubit pairs with improved Bell-state fidelity, with the improvements confirmed in independent hardware runs.
- The work used Quantum Machines’ control and calibration infrastructure alongside NVIDIA accelerated computing, and FirstQFM plans to expand its optimizations as QuantWare develops larger quantum processors.
PRESS RELEASE — FirstQFM today announced results from applying FirstQFM’s quantum foundation model to a QuantWare superconducting quantum processor at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center (IQCC).
FirstQFM’s foundation model builds on top of Quantum Machines’ native calibration stack, and generated single-qubit gates that reduced execution time by 33% on a QuantWare Contralto-D21 QPU. Gates were validated directly on the QuantWare processor using randomized benchmarking with no loss of gate fidelity. The model generated custom pulse-level implementations of gates from calibration data produced by the Quantum Machines’ calibration stack with no additional quantum hardware measurements required. This shifts more of the gate optimization process from scarce QPU time to classical compute.
The model also identified improvements to two-qubit gates, which are central to entanglement and typically more challenging to calibrate than single-qubit operations. Using existing calibration data together with a short hardware probe, the model identified five qubit pairs with higher Bell-state fidelity with each improvement confirmed in independent hardware runs.
The QuantWare processor was operated at the IQCC using Quantum Machines’ OPX control hardware, QUA software, and automated calibration infrastructure. FirstQFM developed its foundation model using NVIDIA accelerated computing hardware and software, including the Leonardo supercomputer and the NVIDIA CUDA-Q open source hybrid platform, before fine-tuning and applying the model to the QuantWare processor.
“FirstQFM’s proprietary, patented foundation models are built to learn the operating characteristics of quantum hardware and use that information to improve how the system performs,” said Vish Ramakrishnan, CEO and Co-Founder of FirstQFM. “On QuantWare’s processor, our model was able to use existing calibration data to generate shorter single-qubit gates while preserving fidelity, and to improve selected two-qubit operations.”
As superconducting quantum processors grow, calibration becomes a harder control problem. More qubits and couplers introduce more operating parameters, device interactions, crosstalk and drift to characterize and manage. FirstQFM plans to expand the set of optimizations available for the 21-qubit device while scaling the solution in preparation for QuantWare advances toward larger VIO-based QPUs.

texto_fonte:
Googlebooks are here, promising productivity aplenty within the Google ecosystem. But how do Google’s new productivity features compare versus the more familiar Windows 11?
That’s the goal for Smart Mode this week: examining how you (and I) can use Googlebooks as productivity devices, specifically looking at several of the features both offer.
Unfortunately, two of the most novel platforms the PC has seen in years — the Googlebook and the Nvidia RTX Spark platform — have landed on the PC within a week or so of each other. I would have liked to have been part of the Googlebook launch, but it took place in my colleague Michael Crider’s backyard, and he already has an extensive professional history covering Android devices. My colleague Ashley Biancuzzo was first out of the gate with our review of the Acer Googlebook 14. (She did a terrific job. Read it! I definitely did.)
My own review is a work in progress…and you’re reading some of it right now.
I’m currently typing this on Lenovo’s Googlebook 15, which I’m crushed to find has an uncharacteristically crappy keyboard. So far, I have few complaints about the hardware, which wasn’t expected to be the star of the show, anyway. Instead, I’m focused on Google’s new Aluminium OS, driving the next evolutionary step of Chromebook devices. It really feels that Google set out to make AI-powered productivity the start of this show.
Welcome to PCWorld’s newsletter, Smart Mode! The focus of this newsletter is productivity: from software to hardware to peripherals, all with the idea to get what you need to get done, efficiently.
I’m your host, Mark Hachman, covering the productivity tips, tools, and trends that you need to know about, both from within PCWorld and beyond. If you want the latest issue in your inbox each week, just sign up right here.
The phone problem
A key part of the productivity equation, however, is that your Googlebook demands an Android phone, and specifically an Android 17 phone at that. Only recently did Google allow rival Samsung phones to connect, but — my Samsung Galaxy S23 is up to date and supported, and it still runs just Android 16. Unexpectedly, that gives Windows a leg up here.
Mark Hachman / Foundry
Phone Link (once called Your Phone) is Windows’ own version of “Better Together,” the corresponding Googlebook technology that connects an Android phone to a Windows PC. Interestingly, Windows only requires Android 10 as an OS requirement to connect the two devices; Googlebooks still have that pesky Android 17 requirement. Without it, phones and Googlebooks still live separate lives. Phone Link allows you to transfer photos from the phone to the PC, place calls and send messages (via Bluetooth) and even run Android phone apps within PC windows.
From what I’ve seen, Phone Link is Googlebook’s surprising equal in all ways except the app streaming. However, Windows can get fussy about which phones support this particular feature, while Googlebooks promise that all compatible phones will support it, with that Android 17 caveat of course.
But Android isn’t always the answer. Outlook works fine on a Windows PC; on my Googlebook, the Googlebook runs the Android app, which took forever to set up my work account. Even worse, it made me re-authenticate every time I logged on. It then crashed.
Windows, meanwhile, secures the entire OS with Windows Hello or a password, and leaves Outlook open to use. (The Lenovo Googlebook includes both face and fingerprint logins in front of an optional PIN, which I like.)
Are Googlebooks smarter? Maybe
Apps may be problematic, but I love how Google has moved widgets forward. On Windows PCs, they’re a distraction, so much that they’re relegated to a closed window in the corner of your screen. On Googlebooks, widgets live on the desktop, where you can create and modify widgets to show whatever information you’d like.
Mark Hachman / Foundry
You can either select from a menu of pre-designed widgets (the screen time widget above is neat) or create your own. This is where AI is going to shine, eventually; you can ask Gemini to create a widget rather than hand-pick features. This doesn’t always work, however. I asked for a “up to the minute widget tracking the MLB playoffs” and received just the scores; I also asked for a widget highlighting all of my priority email and was informed that direct email access isn’t built in. Still, it’s a start.
Microsoft, to is credit, promises something similar with its new Copilot Code feature; I just haven’t played with it at length. Google will probably just make it simpler.
“Simple” also gives Google a slight edge in screen recognition. Magic Pointer and Copilot Vision fall in to the same category of AI assistance to highlight and explain what’s on your screen. Launching the Magic Pointer is more fun when you wiggle your mouse pointer instead of trying to remember another shortcut, for one. Magic Pointer launches a context-aware Gemini that highlights and “knows” what your mouse is pointing toward, and you can ask questions about it. Copilot Vision, hidden within Copilot, takes a different approach, always watching what you’re seeing once you turn it on.
Each has its flaws. Copilot Vision was relatively poor at identifying what it could see. Magic Pointer, though, took close to a full minute using its own “Flash-Lite” engine. Unacceptable!
I’d give Google a clear win for “Rambler,” its voice dictation system. Both Windows and Googlebooks have their own dictation system; Windows has one that’s shared across the platform as well as a dedicated dictation function in Word. Windows 11’s version, though, is pretty literal. Rambler, on the other hand, accommodates the user’s verbal fry (those “um,” “er,” “you know” placeholders we all use) and smooths them out.
One of the ways in which you can enable Rambler is by using the CAPS LOCK key, which Google has repurposed as sort of a shortcut for these little utilities. It’s incredibly useful. Most people don’t actually use the Caps Lock key, and in a situation like this, you can go ahead and cram a number of functions into a single key press. In fact, I dictated most of these last few paragraphs using Rambler, and it inserted punctuation, broke up the sentences, and applied the proper punctuation. That’s AI done right!
Mark Hachman / Foundry
The Googlebook showed me a way to automatically apply AI to the search function within its Files app, promising to append (not rename) all of the files with an AI description. I haven’t seen this happen again, and I’m less concerned about what the AI thinks of how the file should be described than if I can find it, period. Window 11’s own semantic search and its recent changes to the Search function, period, seem just as promising or more so.
What I discovered while using the Googlebook, however, is that Windows is chock full of different ways to perform the same task, simply because it meets the user halfway. I felt like an idiot when I couldn’t find how to reboot the Googlebook (the power button did it). Why does the CAPS LOCK shortcut only work in certain scenarios, like Gmail, but not in others? I also felt a little nervous when absolutely nothing happened while right-clicking the desktop.
So what feels more productive? If I had to compare a Lenovo Windows machine (my demo Panther Lake laptop) versus the Googlebook, I’d definitely choose the Windows machine. The keyboard is far superior, and even with 16GB the Googlebook felt somewhat choppy and laggy. While I can use the Googlebook in the context I normally do — two displays, plus the Googlebook sitting beneath — running a few apps and Chrome tabs felt a lot choppier than I expected. And I still have no idea on the exact battery life, as there’s no great way to track it. Maybe a custom ROM will help?
In an earlier Smart Mode newsletter, I asked who the Googlebook is for? I’m still not entirely sure. I think some of the individual features of the Googlebook are smart, unquestionably. But as a cohesive whole, I still favor my Windows laptop nine times out of ten.
Productivity on camera
I complain about the Googlebook phone issues…but also show off some of the things on Googlebooks that work well, too.
Productivity in the news:
- As busy as I’ve been, the one thing I’ve missed having a chance to try out are the so-called Artcraft apps: AI-generated clones of Adobe’s popular Creative Suite (Photoshop, Premiere, etc.) released as open-source versions coded in Rust. The developer then moved on to the Microsoft 365 apps, pulling off the same trick. The advantages are obvious: no more subscriptions! The disadvantages (copyright infringement, bugs, and so on) have yet to be rooted out.
- Techtober is in full swing, and so we’re involved in trying to evaluate both Googlebooks (again, with Ashley’s terrific review, and mine and others to come) as well as the upcoming RTX Spark laptops — which will cost up to $7,000, yikes! Microsoft has allowed us to confirm that I have a Surface Laptop Ultra on hand, though I can’t say anything about its performance quite yet. I think I’m allowed to say that the keyboard feels a bit tighter than the Surface Laptop Studio, which I haven’t decided is a plus or not.
- If AI is being injected more and more into Windows…it’s going to arrive via Windows Search. I’m not sure who else picked up on this.
- Love is in the air…with laptop stands.
- I thought that the “learn more” Windows local account trick had been patched out years ago?
- It’s worth noting that the AMD Ryzen™ AI Max+ PRO 495 processor will be going up against the new Mediatek-Nvidia RTX Spark partnership for AI workstation notebooks, with up to 192GB (!!) of unified memory. More memory equals bigger AI models, and eventually the two may go head to head.
Productivity tip for the week:
If we’re going to be sticklers for the concept of “productivity,” the most productive days are days when you don’t have to deal with anything else at work… or be at work. Yes, I mean working weekends. I had to do so this weekend and I love the freedom of simply sitting down and fear without fear of someone pinging me for…something. Even my chat requests went unanswered — which they should have!
Just make sure you don’t make a habit of it, or find a manager who will give you compensatory time off in return.
Thanks for reading!
Thanks for tuning in to this edition of Smart Mode, PCWorld’s newsletter devoted to helping you make the most of your life, smartly. Sign up and have it sent to your inbox every Thursday!

Google avisa que vai tirar modelos Pro do plano básico do Gemini
Por Viviane França |
O Google começou a notificar por e-mail os assinantes do plano Google AI Plus de que eles perderão a capacidade de selecionar os modelos Pro no aplicativo Gemini e no Modo IA da Busca, além de perder o acesso aos novos modelos focados em raciocínio. Com a mudança, os usuários interessados em continuar utilizando os modelos mais capazes da empresa terão que fazer um upgrade para o plano Google AI Pro, que custa R$ 96,99 por mês, ou para o plano AI Ultra, a partir de R$ 779,90 por mês.
Com a restrição, os assinantes do plano AI Plus vão ter acesso apenas aos modelos Flash e Flash Lite, que a empresa afirma serem desenvolvidos com foco em velocidade e inteligência. Para as conversas já existentes que utilizaram algum modelo Pro, os usuários poderão dar continuidade ao histórico, mas terão que alternar obrigatoriamente para um modelo diferente para prosseguir com a interação.
Já os usuários do plano gratuito também vão sofrer restrições, com a perda do acesso aos modelos Flash mais recentes, de acordo com a documentação de suporte do Google.
A alteração ocorre em paralelo à expansão da linha de modelos do Google. A empresa anunciou recentemente a disponibilização do Gemini 4 Argon para os assinantes dos níveis AI Pro e AI Ultra, trazendo melhorias em raciocínio, qualidade de escrita e precisão das respostas, além da introdução de novos recursos de gerenciamento de tarefas e integrações com mais de 40 aplicativos.
Quando os modelos Pro serão removidos?
A exclusividade da seleção de modelos Pro para os assinantes do Google AI Pro e planos superiores começará a valer a partir de 13 de novembro de 2026.
Inicialmente, as alterações feitas na documentação de suporte do Gemini no início de outubro indicavam que as restrições de disponibilidade de modelos entrariam em vigor no dia 9 de outubro. Contudo, as notificações enviadas por e-mail aos usuários do plano AI Plus, segundo capturas de tela compartilhadas por usuários do Reddit, confirmaram a data final para 13 de novembro, embora a mensagem do Google não explique o motivo do adiamento no cronograma.

texto_fonte:
Carregar o carro elétrico em casa aumenta quanto na conta de luz?
Por Paulo Amaral |
Uma das principais dúvidas de quem pensa em comprar um carro elétrico é bastante simples: quanto a conta de luz vai aumentar depois que o carro começar a ser carregado em casa? Afinal, a economia com combustível é um dos grandes atrativos dos modelos elétricos, mas a energia usada para abastecer a bateria também tem um custo.
Para descobrir quanto isso representa no bolso, podemos usar como referência o BYD Dolphin Mini, um dos carros elétricos mais conhecidos do mercado brasileiro. A versão equipada com bateria de 38 kWh tem autonomia de até 280 km pelo ciclo do Inmetro, embora o alcance real possa variar de acordo com trânsito, velocidade, temperatura e estilo de condução.
O valor da energia também muda conforme a distribuidora, os impostos e o consumo total da residência. Neste cálculo, a referência é uma casa atendida pela Enel São Paulo em outubro de 2026, considerando a tarifa residencial vigente e a bandeira verde definida pela Aneel para o mês. (Enel)
Quanto custa o kWh em São Paulo em outubro?
Desde 4 de julho de 2026, a tarifa residencial convencional da Enel SP é de R$ 0,78938 por kWh, valor que corresponde à soma da TUSD, de R$ 0,47242/kWh, com a tarifa de energia, de R$ 0,31696/kWh. Esse é o valor homologado para a energia e ainda não considera os impostos que aparecem na conta do consumidor.
Outro ponto importante é que outubro está sob bandeira verde, portanto não há cobrança adicional de bandeira tarifária. Para efeito de cálculo, uma bateria de 38 kWh completamente descarregada e depois carregada até 100% consumiria teoricamente R$ 29,99 em energia. Na prática, o valor pago será maior por causa dos impostos e das perdas do próprio processo de recarga.
Quanto a recarga do Dolphin Mini aumenta a conta?
O cálculo teórico é simples: 38 kWh x R$ 0,78938 = R$ 29,99. Portanto, apenas considerando a tarifa de energia, uma recarga completa do Dolphin Mini acrescentaria cerca de R$ 30 à conta. Como a fatura também inclui tributos, o custo efetivo tende a ficar mais próximo de R$ 1 por kWh em determinadas situações de consumo, o que levaria uma carga completa para algo perto de R$ 38.
Se o motorista percorrer 1.000 km por mês, usando os 280 km de autonomia oficial apenas como referência, seriam necessárias aproximadamente 3,6 cargas completas. Com uma estimativa de R$ 38 por carga, o gasto mensal ficaria perto de R$ 137. O valor real pode variar porque o consumo do carro muda conforme as condições de uso e porque a energia retirada da rede é um pouco maior do que aquela efetivamente armazenada na bateria.
Carregar o carro elétrico em casa compensa?
Mesmo aumentando a conta de luz, o carregamento residencial pode representar uma economia importante para quem deixaria de abastecer um carro a combustão. No exemplo do Dolphin Mini, uma referência de aproximadamente R$ 137 para rodar 1.000 km equivale a cerca de R$ 0,14 por quilômetro, embora o resultado real dependa das condições de uso.
Por isso, quem está avaliando um carro elétrico não deve olhar apenas para o aumento da fatura. A conta de luz sobe, mas é preciso comparar esse valor com o dinheiro que deixa de ser gasto em gasolina ou etanol. Para quem pode carregar o veículo em casa e roda bastante, a diferença tende a pesar positivamente na conta mensal.

candidato.titulo: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
candidato.resumo: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

texto_fonte:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
